doc_description: Walmart Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2019 (formerly Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.) detailing its three-segment omnichannel business and $514.4B in revenues, major portfolio actions (majority acquisition of Flipkart and sale of 80% of Walmart Brazil), rapid U.S. grocery pickup/delivery expansion, share repurchases and market risks, and significant legal matters (Asda equal-value pay claims, opioid litigation, and ongoing FCPA investigations with a $283M accrual), with full MD&A, controls, financial statements, and exhibits.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC Form 10-K filing for Walmart Inc. for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2019 (Commission File No. 001-6991), including issuer details: Delaware incorporation, EIN 71-0415188, principal office in Bentonville, Arkansas, and contact information.
- Securities listing: common stock and certain notes (1.900% due 2022, 2.550% due 2026) registered on the New York Stock Exchange; no Section 12(g) securities.
- Registrant status and compliance: well-known seasoned issuer, large accelerated filer, in compliance with required reports and Interactive Data Files, not a shell company.
- Market and capital structure data: non-affiliate market value as of July 31, 2018 (~$126.8B) and shares outstanding as of March 26, 2019 (2,869,684,230).
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the Proxy Statement for the June 5, 2019 Annual Meeting incorporated into Part III.
- Corporate naming note: company known as Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. prior to February 1, 2018; renamed Walmart Inc. as of that date.
- Table of contents outlining Part I–IV items, including: Business; Risk Factors; Unresolved Staff Comments; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market for Equity and Share Repurchases; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements; Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants; Controls and Procedures; Directors and Governance; Executive Compensation; Security Ownership; Certain Relationships; Accounting Fees; Exhibits; and 10-K Summary.
- Cautionary Statement Regarding Forward-Looking Statements: invocation of the Exchange Act safe harbor; explanation of the nature of forward-looking statements; illustrative areas covered (business growth, financial metrics and operating measures, capital investments and financing, eCommerce and omni-channel initiatives, FX and fuel volatility, shareholder returns via buybacks/dividends, liquidity and funding, hedging, effective tax rate and deferred taxes, litigation impacts, effects of new accounting standards, and sustainability commitments); and common terminology used to identify such statements.

structure.start_phrase:

structure.summary:
- Document type and period: Walmart Inc. Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2019; includes references to the company’s name change from “Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.” to “Walmart Inc.” effective February 1, 2018.
- Forward-looking statements: Defines the nature of such statements, examples of topics covered (growth, financial metrics, investments, eCommerce initiatives, shareholder returns, liquidity, hedging, taxes, litigation, accounting standards, sustainability), typical identifying words/phrases, and underlying assumptions.
- Risks and uncertainties: Extensive caution on factors that could cause actual results to differ, grouped into:
  - Economic factors (global conditions, FX, interest and wage rates, inflation/deflation, energy/transport costs, commodity prices, consumer behavior and confidence, competitor activity, healthcare reimbursement).
  - Operating factors (currency mix of sales/expenses, segment performance and cash flow, traffic and ticket, merchandise mix, supplier availability/costs, strategy execution, integration of acquisitions—especially eCommerce, shrink, customer acceptance of omni-channel, margins incl. pharmacy, fuel prices, seasonality, FCPA and compliance costs, supply chain and cybersecurity disruptions, labor and insurance costs, workforce dynamics, legal/regulatory proceedings, credit ratings, effective tax rate, accounting estimates).
  - Regulatory/other factors (changes in tax/labor laws, tariffs/trade restrictions, government policies, currency controls, public assistance levels, U.S. government shutdowns, timing of tax refunds, natural disasters/public health/civil unrest/terrorism, changes in U.S. GAAP).
  - Notes disproportionate Q4 operating income due to seasonality.
- No duty to update: Advises readers to consider all disclosed risks and states Walmart undertakes no obligation to update forward-looking statements except as required by law.
- Business overview: Mission to help people save money and live better through integrated omni-channel retail; focus on making life easier for busy families, operational discipline, digital transformation, and trust; EDLP pricing and EDLC cost structure at the core.
- Scale and reach: Serves ~275 million customers weekly across 11,300+ stores and numerous eCommerce sites under 58 banners in 27 countries.
- Segments and fiscal calendar: Three reportable segments—Walmart U.S., Walmart International, and Sam’s Club; U.S. and Canada on a fiscal year ending Jan 31; other operations consolidated generally on a one-month lag/calendar basis.
- Fiscal 2019 results and corporate info: Total revenues of $514.4 billion (net sales $510.3 billion); headquarters in Bentonville, Arkansas; common stock ticker WMT on NYSE.
- Company development: Historical milestones from 1945 origins to first discount store (1962), Sam’s Club (1983), supercenter (1988), Neighborhood Market (1998), and international expansion starting 1991 (26 countries as of Jan 31, 2019).
- eCommerce evolution: Launch of walmart.com and samsclub.com (2000), Site to Store (2007), acquisitions and alliances including Jet.com, JD.com (2016), Shoes.com, Moosejaw, Bonobos; free two-day shipping and Store No 8 (2017); majority stake in Flipkart in fiscal 2019 (including Myntra and Jabong ecosystem).
- Omni-channel execution: Rapid expansion of U.S. grocery pickup (>2,100 locations) and delivery (~800 locations) by Jan 31, 2019; building an ecosystem leveraging stores, services, eCommerce, supply chain, and ~2.2 million associates.
- Segment information and geography: Operations across the U.S., Africa, Argentina, Canada, Central America, Chile, China, India, Japan, Mexico, and the U.K.; note on prior Brazil presence and sale of majority stake; segments reviewed by the CODM; generally consistent contribution to sales and operating income with FX-driven variability in International; similar products/services across segments and impracticality of revenue disaggregation by individual product/service.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1 Business
structure.start_phrase: Walmart Inc. ("Wa lmart," the "Company" or "we") helps people around the world save money and live better – anytime and anywhere – by providing the opportunity to shop in retail stores and througheCommerce.
structure.summary:
- Company overview and strategy: Walmart’s mission (save money, live better), omnichannel focus integrating stores and eCommerce, EDLP/EDLC pricing and cost philosophies, trust and convenience as competitive advantages. Scale highlights: ~275 million weekly customers, 11,300+ stores, 58 banners in 27 countries. FY2019 total revenues $514.4B (net sales $510.3B). NYSE: WMT.
- Corporate development timeline: Origins from 1945; first discount store (1962), Sam’s Club (1983), supercenter (1988), Neighborhood Market (1998). International entry in Mexico (1991); presence in 26 countries by Jan 31, 2019. eCommerce milestones: walmart.com and samsclub.com (2000), Site to Store (2007), Jet acquisition and JD.com alliance (2016), acquisitions of Shoes.com, Moosejaw, Bonobos; free two-day shipping and Store No 8 (2017); majority stake in Flipkart (2019). Rapid U.S. grocery pickup/delivery expansion (~2,100 pickup, ~800 delivery locations by Jan 31, 2019).
- Reportable segments and reporting: Walmart U.S., Walmart International, Sam’s Club. Segment performance measured by net sales and operating income; periodic changes to corporate overhead allocations (revised in FY2019 with reclass of prior periods).
- Walmart U.S. segment:
  - Scale and performance: Net sales $331.7B in FY2019 (65% of consolidated), with historically highest gross profit rate among segments.
  - Omnichannel services: Walmart Pickup, Pickup Today, Grocery Pickup and Delivery, Endless Aisle; websites include walmart.com, jet.com, others.
  - Store formats and footprint: Supercenters, Discount Stores, Neighborhood Markets; size ranges and multi-year counts/square feet provided (as of FY2019: 3,570 supercenters; 386 discount stores; 813 neighborhood markets; total ~704.7M sq. ft.).
  - Merchandise: Three strategic units—Grocery; Health & Wellness; General Merchandise (Entertainment, Hardlines, Apparel, Home/Seasonal). Significant private labels (e.g., Great Value, Equate, Mainstays, George, Parent’s Choice, Time and Tru, Wonder Nation, Bonobos) and licensed brands.
  - Operations: Many locations 24/7; seasonal peaks in quarter ending Jan 31.
  - Competition and positioning: Competes with omnichannel retailers across formats and pure-play eCommerce; relies on EDLP, EDLC, and omnichannel convenience.
  - Distribution: ~77% of store merchandise via 156 U.S. distribution centers; private fleet and common carriers; eCommerce fulfilled from 33 dedicated FCs.
- Walmart International segment:
  - Scope and formats: Operations in 26 countries via wholly- and majority-owned subsidiaries; formats include supercenters, supermarkets, hypermarkets, warehouse clubs, cash & carry, and eCommerce (e.g., asda.com, walmart.ca, walmart.com.mx, flipkart.com).
  - Performance: Net sales $120.8B in FY2019 (24% of consolidated); lower gross margin than U.S. due to mix; FX a headwind.
  - Strategic actions: Majority acquisition of Flipkart (2018; negative near-term net income impact), proposed Asda–Sainsbury combination (uncertain regulatory outcome; potential loss upon held-for-sale classification), sale of 80% of Walmart Brazil (pre-tax loss recorded), divestiture of Chile banking ops and proposed divestiture of Canada banking ops.
  - Omnichannel: Click & Collect (UK), grocery pickup/delivery across markets, marketplaces (Flipkart).
  - Footprint detail: Unit counts and square footage by region; total units 5,993 as of Jan 31, 2019 across retail, wholesale, and other (e.g., UK gas stations).
  - Merchandise: Blend of global private brands (e.g., Great Value, George, Equate, Marketside, Parent’s Choice) and market-specific brands (e.g., Aurrera, Lider, Myntra, Jabong, PhonePe, Extra Special); strong local sourcing.
  - Operations and seasonality: Hours and payment methods vary by market; peak in fiscal Q4; competition across retail formats and online; EDLP emphasis.
  - Distribution: 226 distribution facilities across key countries; ~83% of purchases flow through DCs; 90 eCommerce FCs and 1,900+ sort centers in India.
- Sam’s Club segment:
  - Model and scale: Membership-only warehouse clubs in 44 U.S. states and Puerto Rico; net sales $57.8B in FY2019 (11% of consolidated); membership income is significant to operating income.
  - Membership tiers: Plus ($100) and Club ($45); Plus includes Cash Rewards ($10 per $500, up to $500/yr), free shipping on most items, and health/optical discounts; add-on memberships available.
  - Omnichannel: samsclub.com and mobile apps with delivery and Club Pickup; Scan & Go mobile checkout.
  - Footprint: 599 clubs and ~80.2M sq. ft. by FY2019 after prior-year closures.
  - Merchandise categories: Grocery & consumables; Fuel & other; Home & apparel; Technology/office/entertainment; Health & wellness. Member’s Mark private brand exceeded $12B sales in FY2019.
  - Operations and seasonality: Standard and early hours for Plus members; peak in fiscal Q4; competition with Costco and broader retail/eCommerce.
  - Distribution: ~70% of non-fuel purchases via 23 dedicated DCs and some Walmart U.S. DCs; 6 eCommerce FCs plus other DCs (including import); cross-docking focus; mixed fleet/common carriers.
- Intellectual property: Portfolio of trademarks, copyrights, patents, domain names, proprietary technologies; uses legal protections and selective licensing.
- Suppliers and supply chain: Global network of 100,000+ suppliers; significant purchasing leverage; local sourcing for fresh; supplier standards on labor, safety, and laws; in-stock and assortment depend on supplier performance and logistics.
- Employees: >2.2 million associates worldwide (1.5M U.S., 0.7M international). Noted improvement in U.S. turnover; broad benefits (discounts or Sam’s membership, performance bonuses, ESPP match, insurance, healthcare, maternity/parental leave, adoption assistance, tuition support); varied international benefits by locale; retirement-related info referenced.
- Executive leadership: List of executive officers with roles (CEO, CFO, heads of U.S., International, Sam’s Club, U.S. eCommerce, Corporate Affairs, Legal/Governance, People, Controller).
- Investor information: Corporate website; availability of SEC filings and key governance documents; disclosure of ethics code amendments.
- Risk factors (partial): Strategic risks including macroeconomic conditions (interest rates, energy costs, employment, consumer income/debt, credit availability, inflation/deflation, housing, taxes, healthcare, tariffs/trade barriers, FX, recessions) that can dampen demand, alter mix, increase costs, and impact suppliers; intense competition across formats and digital channels on price, assortment, convenience, experience, and delivery speed/cost.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
The risks described below could m
aterially and adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and liquidity.
structure.summary:
- Company website and investor resources: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, proxy materials) and ethics documents (Code of Ethics, Statement of Ethics) are available free on www.stock.walmart.com; printed copies available via Investor Relations. Any substantive amendments/waivers to ethics codes for senior officers will be disclosed online for 12 months. SEC filings also available at www.sec.gov.
- Strategic risks:
  - Macroeconomic pressures (interest rates, fuel/energy costs, inflation/deflation, taxes, healthcare laws, tariffs/trade barriers, unemployment, consumer credit/spending shifts, FX rates) may reduce demand, alter product mix/margins, and increase costs.
  - Intense competition from retailers, eCommerce/omni-channel players, and wholesale clubs; industry consolidation could strengthen rivals.
  - Risk of misreading or lagging consumer trends and shopping patterns.
  - Execution risks and near-/long-term cost impacts of omni-channel and eCommerce investments; potential store traffic cannibalization.
  - Uncertain performance and returns from strategic alliances and business relationships.
- Operational risks:
  - Natural disasters, climate change, and geopolitical events can disrupt facilities, supply chains, utilities, workforce access, transportation, and digital platforms, causing losses and business interruption.
  - Supplier-related risks: compliance with laws/standards, political/economic instability, logistics/port issues, raw material availability, product safety/quality, currency, transport cost/security, sanctions/tariffs/trade limits.
  - Product safety and marketplace risks: liability, reputational harm, and legal exposure, including for third-party (marketplace) sales and potential counterfeit/fraudulent goods.
  - Information systems dependence: outages, cyber-attacks, system changes/migrations, and lack of full redundancy could disrupt operations and increase costs.
  - Digital platform performance and cybersecurity: need for secure, user-friendly online and mobile experiences; exposure to denial-of-service, data theft, reputational harm, lost sales, and competitive erosion.
  - Data privacy and payment security: evolving cyber threats; third-party service provider risks; regulatory noncompliance could trigger litigation, fines, remediation costs, PCI liabilities, and operational disruption.
  - Retail pharmacy risks: reimbursement pressure, payer mix/formulary changes, PBM network dynamics, drug cost/price trends, administrative burden, brand-to-generic shifts, regulatory changes (Medicare/Medicaid/ACA), competition/consolidation, and supply disruptions; potential loss of cross-merchandise sales.
  - Workforce risks: attracting/retaining qualified associates; rising wages/benefits; changing labor and healthcare laws.
- Financial risks:
  - Foreign currency translation and transaction exposure affecting reported results and gross margins.
  - Stock price volatility from missing market expectations or changes to dividends/buybacks; relative underperformance vs. peers.
- Legal, tax, regulatory, compliance, reputational and other risks:
  - International exposure across Africa, Argentina, Canada, Central America, Chile, China, India, Japan, Mexico, and the UK, including political/economic instability, regulatory constraints (including eCommerce limits), data protection, labor, tax, trade, and inflation/devaluation; Brexit-related uncertainties.
  - Anti-corruption compliance risks (FCPA/UK Bribery Act) despite global policies and programs.
  - Tax and trade law changes (tariffs, trade agreements) and U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act uncertainties; audit/review risk; potential material impacts on tax provision, earnings, and cash flows.
  - Broad regulatory regime: U.S. and foreign pharmacy/healthcare (DEA, FDA, Medicare/Medicaid, HIPAA), environmental/health & safety, consumer protection (FTC, CPSC), antitrust/competition, labor/employment, and financial services/AML requirements; potential penalties, exclusions, license loss, and increased compliance costs for noncompliance or changing rules/enforcement.
- Legal proceedings:
  - U.S. class actions (wage/hour, consumer) and UK Asda “equal value” pay claims; outcomes and potential losses not currently estimable.
  - Participation in U.S. opioid multidistrict litigation (MDL 2804) and related state cases seeking damages and injunctive relief.
  - Further details referenced in Item 3 and Note 10.
- FCPA matter:
  - Ongoing DOJ/SEC investigations; $283 million accrual recorded; potential for fines, penalties, injunctions, or other sanctions; continued costs and reputational scrutiny; timing/outcome uncertain, potential future materiality cannot be ruled out.
- Unresolved SEC staff comments: none.

structure.title: Unresolved Staff Comments
structure.heading: Item 1B Unresolved Staff Comments
structure.start_phrase: null.
structure.summary:
- The company faces numerous “equal value” pay claims in the UK against its subsidiary Asda, alleging female store employees perform work of equal value to male warehouse/distribution workers and seeking back pay and higher prospective wages; the number of claims and potential losses cannot be estimated.
- The company is a defendant in the National Prescription Opiate Litigation (MDL No. 2804) in the Northern District of Ohio and in related state cases brought by governments, healthcare providers, tribes, individuals, and third-party payors, seeking compensatory and punitive damages and injunctive/abatement relief; the scope and potential losses are not presently estimable.
- Ongoing FCPA investigations by the U.S. DOJ and SEC have led the company to record a $283 million accrual in fiscal 2018; related Mexican governmental inquiries involved cooperation by Walmex, and shareholder lawsuits tied to these matters have been resolved or have immaterial proposed settlement accruals.
- Potential outcomes include fines, penalties, injunctions, debarment, criminal sanctions, adverse judgments in shareholder suits, reputational harm, and continued costs of investigations and litigation; while the company does not currently expect a material adverse effect, timing and terms of resolution are uncertain and future material impacts are possible.
- References are made to additional detail in Item 3 (Legal Proceedings) and Note 10 to the Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Item 1B (Unresolved Staff Comments): None.

structure.title: Properties
structure.heading: Item 2 Properties
structure.start_phrase:
The Walmart U.S. and Sam's Club segments 
comprise the Company's operations in the U.S.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Excerpts from Walmart’s Annual Report (Form 10-K) covering Item 2 (Properties) and Item 3 (Legal Proceedings), plus environmental disclosures, with store and facility counts largely as of January 31, 2019 (international mostly December 31, 2018, except Canada).

- U.S. properties and unit counts:
  - Detailed, state-by-state counts for Walmart U.S. and Sam’s Club across formats: Supercenters, Discount Stores, Neighborhood Markets/other small formats, and Clubs.
  - U.S. totals: 5,368 units, including 3,570 Supercenters, 386 Discount Stores, 813 Neighborhood Markets/other small formats (comprising 698 Neighborhood Markets, 77 eCommerce retail locations, 38 other small formats), and 599 Sam’s Clubs.

- International operations:
  - Country/region unit counts by category (Retail, Wholesale, Other). Totals: 5,993 units (5,669 Retail, 306 Wholesale, 18 Other).
  - Market highlights: Mexico (2,442), Central America (811), U.K. (633), China (443), Canada (411), Chile (371), Japan (332), Africa (436), Argentina (92), India (22 wholesale only). “Other” includes stand-alone gas stations.
  - Footnotes provide country-level detail for Africa and Central America and note the differing balance sheet dates for unit counts.

- Owned and leased properties; distribution network:
  - Breakout of retail units and distribution facilities (including return facilities and dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers) by ownership/operation type (owned and operated; owned and third-party operated; leased and operated; third-party owned and operated).
  - U.S. retail units: 4,588 owned and operated; 780 leased and operated (total 5,368).
  - U.S. distribution facilities: 179 total (114 owned and operated; 5 owned/third-party operated; 33 leased and operated; 27 third-party owned/operated).
  - International retail units: 1,946 owned and operated; 4,047 leased and operated (total 5,993).
  - International distribution facilities: 226 total (33 owned and operated; 5 owned/third-party operated; 122 leased and operated; 66 third-party owned/operated).
  - Grand totals: 11,361 retail units; 405 distribution facilities; 11,766 total properties (6,681 owned and operated; 10 owned/third-party operated; 4,982 leased and operated; 93 third-party owned/operated).

- Corporate real estate and leasing practices:
  - Principal offices owned in Bentonville, Arkansas; additional offices owned and leased in the U.S. and internationally.
  - Store land is owned or leased; buildings constructed by independent contractors.
  - Leases include annual rent (with possible escalations and percentage rent based on sales) and typically offer renewal options, some with escalation clauses.
  - Reference to segment “Distribution” sections for additional detail.

- Legal proceedings (Item 3):
  - Cross-reference to Note 10 “Contingencies” and listing of key matters.
  - ASDA Equal Value Claims (U.K.): multiple proceedings in the Manchester Employment Tribunal, Employment Appeal Tribunal, and Court of Appeal.
  - National Prescription Opiate Litigation (MDL No. 2804), N.D. Ohio: 440 cases in MDL as of March 15, 2019; 27 pending transfer/remand; 92 additional state cases (listed in Exhibit 99.1).
  - Securities Class Action: City of Pontiac General Employees Retirement System v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. (alleged FCPA-related securities violations tied to 2012 reporting). Class certified Sept. 20, 2016; Eighth Circuit denied petition to appeal Nov. 7, 2016. Proposed $160 million settlement filed Oct. 26, 2018; preliminarily approved Dec. 6, 2018; no admission of wrongdoing; settlement expensed in fiscal 2019.

- Environmental matters (Item 103, Reg S-K):
  - EPA Draft Consent Agreement and Final Order alleging distribution/sale of three unregistered pesticide products (Mar 1–Jun 23, 2017); proposed $960,000 penalty; company cooperating and notes manufacturer responsibility for product registration.
  - Mexico (State of Chiapas) fine of ~US$163,000 for absence of an Environmental Impact Authorization License at Mi Bodega Las Rosas; company is contesting the fine.
  - Management does not believe potential losses, individually or in aggregate, are material to financial condition or results of operations.

structure.title: Legal Proceedings
structure.heading: Item 3 Legal Proceedings
structure.start_phrase:
We discuss certain leg al proceedings in Note 10 to our Consolidated Financial Sta tements, entitled "Contingencies," which is included in Part II, Item 8. Financial Statements and Suppl
elementary Data of this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
structure.summary:
- Properties: Company-owned principal offices in Bentonville, Arkansas, with additional owned and leased offices in the U.S. and internationally. Store sites are either owned or leased; leases include annual rent with potential escalations and percentage rent based on sales, and most have renewal options that may also escalate. Buildings are constructed by independent contractors. Distribution center details are provided elsewhere under segment “Distribution.”
- Legal proceedings (supplemental information; see Note 10, “Contingencies,” for full details):
  - ASDA Equal Value Claims: Multiple related cases in the UK (Manchester Employment Tribunal, Employment Appeal Tribunal, and Court of Appeal) involving equal value pay claims.
  - National Prescription Opiate Litigation: Participation in MDL No. 2804 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio; as of March 15, 2019, 440 cases included, 27 in transfer/remand status, and 92 additional state cases (listed in Exhibit 99.1).
  - Securities Class Action: City of Pontiac General Employees Retirement System v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., alleging securities law violations tied to FCPA-related disclosures following an April 21, 2012 New York Times article. Class certified; Eighth Circuit denied petition to appeal. Proposed $160 million settlement filed Oct. 26, 2018, preliminarily approved Dec. 6, 2018, with a final approval hearing set for April 4, 2019; no admission of wrongdoing; settlement expensed in fiscal 2019.
- Environmental matters (Item 103, Regulation S-K): Management does not believe potential losses, individually or in aggregate, are material.
  - EPA (U.S.): Draft Consent Agreement/Final Order alleging sale/distribution of three unregistered pesticide products (Mar 1–Jun 23, 2017); penalty sought $960,000; company cooperating.
  - Mexico (Chiapas): Approximately $163,000 fine for absence of an Environmental Impact Authorization for a store; company challenging.
  - California ARB: Dispute over ~$4.2 million in unclaimed deposits from small automotive refrigerant containers; ARB asserts funds must support consumer education; company denies wrongdoing.
  - Costa Rica (Curridabat): Approximately $380,000 penalty related to a retaining wall near a protected river bank for a perishables distribution center; permits were obtained at construction; municipality now alleges non-conformance.
- Mine safety disclosures: Not applicable.

structure.summary:
- Regulatory and legal matters: California Air Resources Board claims retailers must use unclaimed deposits from small automotive refrigerant containers for consumer education; alleges the company retained ~$4.2 million. The company denies wrongdoing. In Costa Rica, a subsidiary faces a proposed ~$380,000 municipal penalty related to a retaining wall near a protected river bank; permits were obtained, but the wall is now alleged to be non‑conforming.
- Mine safety disclosures: Not applicable.
- Market information: Walmart common stock trades on the NYSE under “WMT.” As of March 26, 2019, there were 223,968 holders of record.
- Stock performance: Five-year cumulative total return comparison (2014–2019) versus the S&P 500 and S&P 500 Retailing Index, assuming $100 invested with dividends reinvested; FY2019 values shown include Walmart at $146.06 versus S&P 500 at $168.19 and S&P 500 Retailing at $256.26.
- Share repurchases: Ongoing buybacks under a $20.0 billion authorization approved in October 2017 with no expiration; $11.3 billion remained authorized as of January 31, 2019. Repurchased shares are retired.

structure.title: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7 Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
This discussion, which presents our resu
lts for the fiscal years ended January 31, 2019 ("fiscal 2019 "), January 31, 2018 ("fiscal 2018 ") and January 31, 2017 ("fiscal 2017 ") should be read in conjunction with our Consolidated Finan
cial Statements and the accompanying notes.
structure.summary:
- Management’s Discussion and Analysis for fiscal years ended January 31, 2019, 2018, and 2017, explaining how results are measured and analyzed, including segment operating income, comparable sales (with eCommerce and omni-channel included), currency exchange impacts, and seasonality.
- Strategic portfolio actions:
  - Acquisition of a majority stake in Flipkart (negative impact to FY2019 results and expected into FY2020).
  - Proposed Asda–Sainsbury combination (not classified as held for sale as of year-end; outcomes uncertain).
  - Divestiture of 80% of Walmart Brazil (pre-tax loss ~$4.8B) and banking operations in Chile (completed) and Canada (held for sale).
- Industry context: highly competitive omni-channel retail landscape and macro factors affecting performance (consumer dynamics, tariffs, FX, fuel, labor, cybersecurity, etc.).
- Financial framework and performance metrics:
  - Focus on strong, efficient growth; operating discipline; and strategic capital allocation.
  - Comparable sales results (calendar basis): Walmart U.S. +3.7% (eCommerce contributed ~1.3 pts), Sam’s Club +5.4% (fuel and traffic; club closures mix), Total U.S. +4.0%; note on retail vs fiscal calendar presentation.
  - Expense leverage in FY2019 (OSG&A down 48 bps vs sales) from productivity and lapping FY2018 charges; continued investment in eCommerce/technology and a securities class action charge.
- Capital allocation:
  - Shift of capex toward eCommerce, technology, supply chain, and remodels; fewer new stores/clubs.
  - FY2019 capex ~$10.3B (U.S. ~$7.7B; International ~$2.7B).
- Returns:
  - ROA 3.4% (down due to Brazil divestiture loss and JD.com unrealized loss); ROI 14.2% (non-GAAP), with methodology and reconciliation; note ROI methodology to change with lease accounting adoption.
- Free cash flow:
  - Defined as operating cash flow less capex; FY2019 $17.4B (down vs prior years) driven by vendor payment timing and slightly higher capex.
- Consolidated results:
  - Total revenues and net sales up ~3% in FY2019; gross profit rate down (eCommerce mix, pricing, transportation, Flipkart consolidation).
  - Operating expenses leveraged in FY2019; FY2018 included significant one-time charges.
  - Other losses in FY2019 from Brazil divestiture and JD.com mark-to-market; FY2018 included debt extinguishment losses.
  - Effective tax rate dynamics post–Tax Act; EPS declined in FY2019.
- Segment performance:
  - Walmart U.S.: strong comp growth (traffic and ticket), margin pressure from price/transport/eCommerce mix; expense leverage vs ongoing investments; operating income up modestly.
  - Walmart International: sales up on comps and Flipkart; offset by Brazil sale and FX; gross margin down (Flipkart, price investments); lower membership/other income vs prior-year gains; operating income down.
  - Sam’s Club: net sales down on club closures and tobacco removal but strong comps (fuel and traffic); margin mixed (lower markdowns, higher transport/eCom shipping, shrink); operating expenses improved vs prior-year closure charges; operating income rebounded.
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Operating cash flow ~$27.8B; cash and equivalents $7.7B; typical working capital deficit improved with Flipkart consolidation.
  - Repatriated ~$5.3B to the U.S.; certain cash not freely transferable (Flipkart minority protections).
  - Investing: FY2019 outflows driven by Flipkart (~$13.8B net of cash); FY2020 capex plan ~$11B with ~300 new International stores (mainly Mexico, Central America, China) and <10 in U.S.
  - Financing: $15.9B net proceeds from long-term debt (partly for Flipkart); reduced buybacks early in FY2019 then normalized; details on short-term borrowings and undrawn credit lines.
  - Long-term debt increased to ~$45.4B; FY2020 dividend set at $2.12/share; ongoing $20B repurchase program with ~$11.3B remaining; FY2019 repurchases ~$7.4B.
  - Strong credit ratings (S&P AA/A-1+, Moody’s Aa2/P-1, Fitch AA/F1+).
- Contractual obligations and commitments:
  - Schedule of debt, leases, interest, letters of credit, and purchase obligations; indemnification to Advent for Brazil pre-closing contingencies; undrawn committed credit lines.
  - Note on unrecognized tax benefits; no material off-balance sheet arrangements.
- Other matters: summaries and cross-references for FCPA investigation, ASDA Equal Value Claims, and National Prescription Opiate Litigation.
- Critical accounting estimates: inventories (RIM/LIFO), long-lived asset impairment approach and sensitivities, business combinations/goodwill and intangible valuations (including areas of potential impairment), income tax judgments/uncertain tax positions/deferred tax assets, and Tax Act effects.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase:
In addition to the risks inhe
rent in our operations, we are exposed to certain market risks, including changes in interest rates, currency exchange rates and the fair value of our equity investment inJD.com.
structure.summary:
- Section overview: Item 7A – Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk, covering exposures to interest rate risk, foreign currency risk, and equity investment valuation risk (JD.com).
- Interest rate risk:
  - Exposure arises from short-term borrowings and long-term debt; risk managed via mix of fixed/variable debt and interest rate swaps.
  - Net fair value of interest rate swaps increased $13 million in fiscal 2019 due to market rate fluctuations.
  - As of January 31, 2019, variable-rate borrowings (including commercial paper and swaps) were 22% of total debt.
  - Sensitivity: a 100 bps change in market rates would change annual interest expense by approximately $110 million.
  - Detailed schedule of debt maturities and weighted-average rates provided; interest rate swaps include $4.0 billion notional fixed-to-variable positions with stated pay/receive rates.
- Foreign currency risk:
  - Exposure from non-U.S. operations, net investments, and foreign-currency-denominated debt.
  - FY2019 currency movements (notably in the UK, Chile, Canada) drove a $2.1 billion loss in currency translation and other AOCI.
  - Currency swaps used to hedge a portion of risk; fair value asset position of $62 million at Jan 31, 2019 (down from $413 million in 2018) due to U.S. dollar strengthening.
  - Sensitivities: a hypothetical 10% change in FX rates underlying the swaps would change swap value by ~$515 million; a 10% change in interest rates underlying the swaps would change value by ~$13 million.
  - Nonderivative net investment hedges: £1.7 billion of UK debt and ¥180 billion of Japan debt designated; a 10% USD move vs. GBP would change debt value by ~$201 million; vs. JPY by ~$150 million.
  - Additional immaterial FX forwards used for purchase commitments.
- Investment risk (JD.com):
  - Equity investment fair value subject to JD.com stock price changes.
  - Following adoption of new financial instruments standard on Feb 1, 2018, changes recognized in other gains and losses; resulted in a $3.5 billion loss in fiscal 2019 due to JD stock decline.
  - Fair value of JD.com investment was $3.6 billion as of January 31, 2019.

structure.title: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.heading: Item 8 Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.start_phrase: We have audited the ac companying consolidated balance sheets of Walmart Inc. (the Company) as of January 31, 2019 and 2018 , the related consolida ted statements of income, comprehensive income,shareholders' equity and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended January 31, 2019 , and the related notes (collectively referred to as the "consolidated financial statements").
structure.summary:
- Independent auditor reports: Ernst & Young LLP issued unqualified opinions on Walmart Inc.’s FY2019, FY2018, and FY2017 consolidated financial statements and on internal control over financial reporting as of January 31, 2019. The ICFR audit excluded Flipkart’s internal controls (except goodwill and intangibles recognition); Flipkart represented ~2% of total assets (ex-goodwill/intangibles) and ~1% of FY2019 net sales.
- Accounting changes: Adoption of ASU 2016-01 (financial instruments) effective Feb 1, 2018 changed measurement of certain equity investments to fair value with changes in earnings; adoption of ASU 2016-18 (restricted cash) in cash flows; adoption of ASC 606 (revenue) with immaterial impact; upcoming ASC 842 (leases) in FY2020 expected to add ~$15B to total assets/liabilities.
- Consolidated results (FY2019): Total revenues $514.4B; net sales $510.3B; operating income $22.0B; net income attributable to Walmart $6.67B; diluted EPS $2.26; dividends declared per share $2.08. Total assets $219.3B; total equity $79.6B; long‑term debt $43.5B (after $15.9B 2018 issuances largely to fund Flipkart). Operating cash flow $27.8B; investing cash outflow $24.0B (Flipkart acquisition, capex); financing cash outflow $2.5B (buybacks, dividends, debt activity).
- Segment highlights (FY2019): Net sales—Walmart U.S. $331.7B (eCommerce ~$15.7B), Walmart International $120.8B (eCommerce ~$6.7B), Sam’s Club $57.8B (eCommerce ~$2.7B). Operating income—Walmart U.S. $17.4B, International $4.9B, Sam’s Club $1.5B. Disaggregated revenue by category/market provided.
- Key business combinations and disposals:
  - Flipkart (India) acquisition: 81% acquired for ~$16B; recognized ~$13.6B goodwill and ~$5.0B intangibles (including $4.7B indefinite‑lived trade names); $4.3B noncontrolling interest; consolidated with one‑month lag.
  - Walmart Brazil: Sold 80% stake; recorded pre‑tax net loss of ~$4.8B (including full impairment of assets held for sale and $2.0B CTA reclassification); indemnity liability recognized; retained 20% interest (equity method at no initial fair value).
  - Other: Proposed Asda/Sainsbury combination pending regulatory outcome; prior Suburbia sale (Mexico) and Yihaodian asset sale to JD (China); Jet.com acquisition (2016).
- Fair value and investments: JD.com investment remeasured under ASU 2016-01; cumulative decrease of ~$3.5B in FY2019 recognized in other gains/losses. Derivatives and net investment hedges detailed with notional amounts and fair values; fair value hierarchy disclosures included.
- Capital structure and liquidity: Short‑term borrowings ~$5.2B; committed U.S. credit lines $15.0B (undrawn at year‑end) plus ~$3.0B international facilities; FY2019 long‑term debt issuances ~$15.9B; scheduled maturities provided; FY2018 debt extinguishment loss ~$3.1B noted.
- Shareholders’ equity: Share repurchases of $7.41B (79.5M shares) under $20B authorization (remaining $11.3B); share‑based compensation expense $773M; detailed award types and activity; AOCI rollforward, including effects from standards adoption and Brazil CTA reclassification.
- Taxation: Provision for income taxes $4.28B; effective tax rate 37.4% (impacted by Brazil disposal, transition tax, valuation allowance changes). Tax Cuts and Jobs Act effects—transition tax finalized (additional $413M expense in FY2019), deferred tax remeasurement updates, GILTI treated as period cost. Deferred tax assets/liabilities and valuation allowances disclosed; uncertain tax positions rollforward.
- Commitments and leases: Operating lease commitments and capital lease/financing obligation schedules presented; note that ASC 842 adoption in FY2020 will significantly increase reported lease assets/liabilities.
- Retirement benefits: U.S. 401(k) and international defined contribution plan expense $1.29B; defined benefit status for UK (overfunded) and Japan (underfunded) plans disclosed.
- Contingencies and legal matters: 
  - Asda equal value pay claims in the UK proceeding to equal value phase; outcomes and potential losses not estimable.
  - Opioid litigation (federal MDL and state cases) and related government inquiries; defenses asserted; losses not estimable.
  - FCPA investigations (DOJ/SEC): prior aggregate accrual of $283M; ongoing compliance enhancements; FY2019 third‑party costs ~$30M.
- Other items: Restructuring charges of $1.2B in FY2018 for Sam’s Club closures and Brazil eCommerce wind‑down; quarterly financial data (unaudited) for FY2019 and FY2018; subsequent event—FY2020 annual dividend set at $2.12 per share (quarterly schedule provided).

structure.summary:
- Context: This is the exhibits section of Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2019, plus the full text of certain filed exhibits.

- Exhibit Index highlights:
  - Corporate governance documents: Restated Certificate of Incorporation (Feb 1, 2018) and Amended & Restated Bylaws (Feb 1, 2018), incorporated by reference.
  - Debt instruments: Base indentures (1991, 2002, 2005) and supplemental indentures (1992, 2006, 2014, 2018) with successor trustees, largely incorporated by reference.
  - Executive/compensation plans (management contracts/compensatory arrangements):
    - Walmart Inc. Officer Deferred Compensation Plan; Management Incentive Plan (MIP); 2016 Associate Stock Purchase Plan; Stock Incentive Plan of 2015; Supplemental Executive Retirement Plan; Director Compensation Deferral Plan; Walmart Deferred Compensation Matching Plan (filed in full here, effective Feb 1, 2019).
    - Various award forms (performance units, restricted stock, RSUs), including annual executive award forms for 2017–2018.
  - Executive agreements and transactions:
    - Post-Termination Agreement and Covenant Not to Compete (with amended schedule of covered executive officers).
    - Agreements related to Marc Lore (share-settled RSUs, deferred contingent merger consideration and amendment, non-compete).
    - Transition and Retirement Agreement for David Cheesewright.
    - Flipkart acquisition documents: Share Issuance and Acquisition Agreement and Share Purchase Agreement (certain portions omitted for confidential treatment).
  - Standard filings:
    - List of Significant Subsidiaries (Exhibit 21).
    - Auditor consent from Ernst & Young LLP (Exhibit 23).
    - CEO/CFO Section 302 certifications (Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2) and Section 906 certifications (Exhibits 32.1 and 32.2).
    - State court prescription opiate litigation case citations as of March 15, 2019 (Exhibit 99.1).
    - XBRL exhibits (instance, schema, calculation, definition, label, presentation).
  - Notes to Exhibit Index:
    - Prior filings available on EDGAR; historical documents can be reviewed at the SEC Public Reference Room.
    - Long-term debt instruments for series under 10% of assets are not filed per Item 601(b)(4)(iii)(A) of Regulation S-K; Walmart agrees to furnish them to the SEC upon request.

- Walmart Deferred Compensation Matching Plan (Amended and Restated Effective Feb 1, 2019) – key provisions:
  - Purpose/nature: Unfunded, nonqualified “top-hat” retirement plan under ERISA for a select group of management/highly compensated employees; intended to comply with IRC Section 409A; benefits paid from Walmart’s general assets.
  - Eligibility/definitions: Covers Eligible Officers (VP and above or equivalent roles) and certain senior employees/market managers or those over the 401(a)(17) compensation cap; detailed definitions for Accounts, Compensation, Excess Compensation, Separation from Service, etc.
  - Deferrals:
    - Base compensation (Section 3.1): Elections due by 12/31 preceding the Plan Year or within 30 days of first becoming eligible; applied per payroll; subject to withholding minimums and 409A rules.
    - MIP bonuses (Section 3.2): Elections generally due before performance period; special timing for 409A “performance-based compensation” and first-time eligible officers.
    - Special bonuses (Section 3.3): Deferrable if tied to pre-employment offer letters referencing the Plan or if subject to ≥13-month service/vesting conditions; specific election timing rules.
  - Employer Matching Contribution Credits (Section 3.4): Credited if employed on the last day of the Plan Year and no separation; match equals total deferrals of base comp and MIP bonus up to 6% of Excess Compensation; vesting after 3 Years of Participation (or upon death/disability); unvested match forfeited; no match on amounts withdrawn for emergencies.
  - Accounts and allocations (Section 3.5): Deferrals allocated to Retirement Accounts and/or Scheduled In‑Service Accounts; matching credits to Retirement Accounts; default allocation rules if elections are missing.
  - Valuation/earnings (Sections 4.3–4.4): Daily valuation; credited simple interest each Valuation Date at 10-year U.S. Treasury yield (as of first business day of January preceding the Plan Year) plus 270 bps.
  - Distributions (Article V):
    - Scheduled In‑Service: Lump sum within 90 days of the elected Scheduled Pay Date (not earlier than the second Plan Year after initial credit); overridden by earlier separation/death.
    - Separation from Service: Six-month delay applies (Separation Pay Date); Scheduled In‑Service Accounts paid in lump sum; Retirement Accounts paid per election as a lump sum (within 90 days after the Separation Pay Date) or annual installments up to 15 years (first installment after Separation Pay Date/next Jan 31; fixed amortization using plan rate).
    - Death: Lump sum or installments to beneficiaries per participant’s election; default to lump sum if no election; continuation rules if death occurs after installments begin; beneficiary designation and default hierarchy provided.
    - Unforeseeable Emergency: Distributions allowed to the extent necessary (with tax gross-up for related taxes), prioritized across accounts; potential suspension of deferrals; 162(m) deduction timing rule through Jan 1, 2021.
    - Tax payments: Limited acceleration for FICA/income tax withholding and certain non-U.S. taxes.
    - Gross Misconduct: Forfeiture of all employer match and reduction of credited interest rate to 50% of plan rate on deferral earnings; clawback of excess payments; deferred principal (deferrals) never forfeited.
  - Administration/claims (Articles VI–VII): Administered by the Compensation and Management Development Committee; powers to interpret, delegate, and establish procedures; strict claims and appeals timelines; disability claims follow DOL Reg. 2560.503‑1.
  - Miscellaneous (Article VIII): 409A-compliant amendment/termination (including change-in-control liquidation requirements); anti-assignment with limited QDRO-style exception (lump sum only); recovery of overpayments; no employment/bonus rights; tax withholding; governing law Delaware.

- Amended Schedule of Executive Officers with Post‑Termination Agreement and Covenant Not to Compete:
  - Identifies executives (e.g., C. Douglas McMillon, M. Brett Biggs, John R. Furner, Gregory Foran, Rachel L. Brand, etc.), agreement dates, and in some cases the value of restricted stock granted in connection (e.g., McMillon $2,000,000; Biggs $500,000; many marked Not Applicable).

- Significant Subsidiaries (selected):
  - U.S.: Wal‑Mart Stores East, LP; Wal‑Mart Stores Texas, LLC; Wal‑Mart Property Company; Wal‑Mart Real Estate Business Trust; Sam’s West, Inc.; Sam’s East, Inc.; Sam’s Property Company; Sam’s Real Estate Business Trust (generally 100% owned).
  - International: ASDA Group Limited (UK, 100%); Wal‑Mart de México, S.A.B. de C.V. (Mexico, 71%); Wal‑Mart Canada Corp. (100%); Flipkart Private Limited (Singapore, 81%); Wal‑Mart Japan Holdings K.K. (100%, Seiyu); Walmart Chile S.A. (substantially all owned); Massmart Holdings Ltd (South Africa, 52%).

- Auditor consent:
  - Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporation by reference of its reports (financial statements and ICFR) into numerous Walmart registration statements (various S‑8 and S‑3 filings); dated March 28, 2019.

- CEO/CFO certifications:
  - Section 302 certifications by C. Douglas McMillon (CEO) and M. Brett Biggs (CFO) regarding disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting.
  - Section 906 certifications by CEO and CFO attesting to the 10‑K’s compliance and fair presentation.

- State court prescription opiate litigation:
  - An exhibit listing numerous pending state and local government and other plaintiffs’ cases against opioid manufacturers/distributors (with dates, courts, and jurisdictions) through March 15, 2019, including actions in New York, Maine, West Virginia, New Hampshire, South Carolina, Illinois, Wisconsin, New Mexico, and others.
